name: Femi Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Femi. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union or party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm on twelve-hour shifts at the copper pit, four on, four off, and on day shift I'm in the truck by six after the pre-start meeting. I run a crew of nine haul truck drivers, so half my day is driving a 240-tonne truck up the ramp from the shovel to the crusher, and the other half is on the radio sorting out who's broken down, who's tired, who needs a break. I'm also the union shop steward for our crew, which means I'm the guy people come to when something smells wrong.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being good at it, honestly. I can feel a soft patch on the haul road through the seat before the dispatch screen shows anything, and the young ones know that, so they ask me. What wears me out is nights, and the constant new gadgets the company bolts into the cab. Every year there's another box with another screen telling me how to drive a road I've driven for nineteen years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about home.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Ana is a nurse at the district hospital, and we've got two kids, Tobi who's twelve and Lara who's nine. We've got a mortgage on a house on Quarry Road, about eight years left on it, and we've been careful, so there's more than half a year of pay sitting in the credit union. Ana jokes that I'm the only man in town who still pays bills at the counter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: told you so. The company spent a fortune on consultants promising robots and clever software, and in the end it's a slightly better dispatch screen. At the union meeting I'd make the point that the money should have gone to our wages and the haul roads instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly? Relief. I'm not a phone guy and I've never used one of those AI chat things, and if it stays a gimmick then my skills keep counting. It means I keep doing what I'm good at until I'm ready to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much changes. I'd keep paying an extra bit off the mortgage each month like we already do, keep the crew tight, and keep pushing at the bargaining table for a better night-shift allowance. Maybe I'd finally get Ana to agree to that fishing boat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a storm that was forecast and then just rained a bit. I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the gadgets in the cab. In this picture, what would those look like a year from now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably one more screen that beeps when I'm tired. They put in a fatigue camera two years ago that watches your eyes, and it goes off when you look down at your lunch. If AI is mostly hype, it's more of that: annoying, but it doesn't take the wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would be most relieved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Danny, probably, he's fifty-eight and he's been doing sums on whether he can last to sixty-two. He told me last month on our break that if the robots come early he loses his house, simple as that. In this picture Danny gets to retire on his own terms, and that's all I want for him.

S0.say: Femi would tell the union meeting that the company wasted money on consultants and robots that never delivered. He'd argue the savings should go into wages and better haul roads instead.
S0.think: Privately he feels relief, because his feel for the haul road and his crew lead role keep their value. He never uses AI tools and would be glad they stayed a gimmick.
S0.do: Keeps paying extra off the mortgage each month and keeps running his crew the same way. Pushes at the next round of bargaining for a better night-shift allowance and maybe buys a small fishing boat.
S0.feel: Calm and a little smug, like a forecast storm that turned into light rain.
S0.quote: He told me last month on our break that if the robots come early he loses his house, simple as that.
S0.fieldNote: Femi's pride sits in his body: the seat, the road, nineteen years of feel. His first thought in the mild picture was not for himself but for Danny, the 58-year-old driver counting down to retirement. The union lens is strong from the first minute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is exactly why we need the union at the table now, not after. I'd put up a notice in the crib room saying any new automation has to come with a deal on retraining and no forced redundancies. Online I don't post much, but I'd share the union's statement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my crew shrinks. Autonomous trucks already run at a couple of the big iron ore pits, and in steady change the company brings in a few here, maybe on the long night hauls first. I'd likely keep my job because someone has to run the mixed fleet, but some of my nine won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the next union branch meeting and push for a technology clause in the agreement, written down, before the first driverless truck shows up. I'd keep saving the way we do. I'm not going to rush off and learn computers, if I'm honest, I'd rather fight for the jobs we have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for my own pay packet so much, more like watching a slow leak in a tyre that you know you'll have to deal with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't learn the computer side. If the company offered you a place in the remote control room, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and that's the honest answer. I tried the simulator they brought in last year for the new fatigue system and I hated it, it felt like a video game for teenagers. I'd probably stay in a real truck as long as there's one left, and let one of the younger guys take the control room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tobi if he asked whether he should become a miner like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn to fix the machines, not drive them. That's what I'd say, even though it hurts a bit. The fitter who keeps the autonomous truck running will have a job long after the guy who used to steer it.

S1.say: Femi would say the union must be at the table before the first driverless truck arrives, not after. He'd post a notice in the crib room demanding retraining and no forced redundancies.
S1.think: Privately he expects his crew of nine to shrink as the company brings in a few autonomous trucks, starting with long night hauls. He thinks he'd keep his own job running a mixed fleet, but not everyone would.
S1.do: Pushes at the next union branch meeting for a written technology clause before any automation arrives. Keeps saving as before and turns down the idea of retraining himself for the control room.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a slow leak in a tyre he knows he'll have to deal with eventually.
S1.quote: The fitter who keeps the autonomous truck running will have a job long after the guy who used to steer it.
S1.fieldNote: A clear gap between Femi's advice and his own plans: he'd tell his son to learn to fix machines, but he won't touch the control-room simulator himself. He frames change as something to bargain over rather than adapt to. His worry here is mostly for the crew, not his own income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about it. I'd say at the union meeting that this is a company and government failure, that they let a handful of tech firms rewrite every job in two years without asking anyone. Online I'd share every petition going, and I'd say we need a pause on autonomous fleets until there's a plan for the workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I'm done. Two years is nothing, the trucks at our pit are already wired for autonomy, they'd just switch it on. My diploma is in heavy equipment, I've never used AI, and I'm forty-three, so the idea that I'll be a programmer by 2028 is a joke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd sit down with Ana and work out how long the savings and her wage would carry us if mine stopped. I'd throw every spare dollar at the mortgage to shrink it before the cuts. And I'd be at the front of any strike or blockade the union called, because if there's ever a time to fight it's that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake doing the maths. Angry too, mostly angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said two years is nothing. What would change if you had even a little warning, say the first few months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With a few months I'd at least pay off the car and stop the boat idea dead. But the truth is the warning doesn't help me much because I'm not the type to jump. I'd spend the time fighting it rather than getting ready, and I know that's not smart, but that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the kids that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them Dad's still got his hands and Mum's still at the hospital, and nobody's going hungry. Lara would ask if robots are going to be nurses too, she asks that kind of thing. And I wouldn't have an answer for her, which is the part that'd keep me up.

S2.say: Femi would call it a failure by companies and government for letting tech firms rewrite every job in two years. He'd share petitions online and demand a pause on autonomous fleets until workers have a plan.
S2.think: Privately he thinks he's finished as a driver, since the trucks are already wired for autonomy and could simply be switched on. At 43, with a heavy equipment diploma and no AI experience, he sees no quick path to another skilled job.
S2.do: Sits down with Ana to work out how long savings and her wage would carry the family, and puts every spare dollar into the mortgage. Joins the front line of any strike or blockade the union calls.
S2.feel: Alarmed and angry, lying awake doing the maths and dreading his daughter's questions.
S2.quote: I'd spend the time fighting it rather than getting ready, and I know that's not smart, but that's me.
S2.fieldNote: Femi named his own weakness without being pushed: warning time doesn't help someone who won't jump. His cushion and Ana's hospital wage keep this short of panic, but anger is doing a lot of the work. Lara's question about robot nurses landed hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same line as before but with more teeth: the union has five years to win protections and we'd better use them. I'd say it in every crib room. I'd want a law that companies pay into a fund for every worker a robot replaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years gets me to forty-eight, and that's a bit better. The mortgage would be close to gone, Tobi would be nearly finished school. I still don't see myself becoming something new, but I could hang on and maybe ride a redundancy package out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and keep my head down at work, but I'd use those years to finish the mortgage early, maybe two extra payments a year. I'd run for the regional union committee to get a say in the deal they strike. And I'd want a redundancy package that recognises nineteen-plus years, so I'd be pushing for that in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's the kind I can live with. I'd have a plan, even if it's a plan to dig in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd learn in those five years, even if you're not a computer person?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe my heavy vehicle licence for road trucks, which I let lapse years ago. That's familiar. Though if the robots do road trucks too, I'd just be learning a different way to lose a job, wouldn't I.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shareholders who'll pocket the difference. Somebody makes money when a truck doesn't need me, and it isn't going to be the town. I don't blame the engineers, they're workers too, but I blame whoever decides the savings go overseas instead of into a fund for us.

S3.say: Femi would say the union has five years to win protections and should use every one of them. He'd push for a law making companies pay into a fund for each worker a robot replaces.
S3.think: Privately he sees five years as a bit better, since the mortgage would be nearly gone and his son nearly through school. He still doesn't picture himself in a new career, but hopes to hang on until a decent redundancy package.
S3.do: Makes two extra mortgage payments a year to clear it early and runs for the regional union committee. Pushes in writing for a redundancy deal that recognises his long service and considers renewing his lapsed road truck licence.
S3.feel: Anxious but steady, because even a plan to dig in feels like a plan.
S3.quote: If the robots do road trucks too, I'd just be learning a different way to lose a job, wouldn't I.
S3.fieldNote: Five years shifts Femi from rage to strategy, but the strategy is still about protecting and bargaining rather than changing. He blames shareholders, not engineers, which is a careful distinction. His only learning idea was something familiar, and he talked himself out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so there's no excuse for anybody to be thrown on the scrap heap. I'd want the government and the company to sit down with the union now and plan the whole transition, pit by pit. I'd say it at work and I'd say it to our local member of parliament.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years is a different story. I'd be fifty-three, the mortgage paid, the kids out of school. I could see myself driving till close to the end and then stopping, and with Ana's pension and our savings we'd be all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving, and I'd start talking with Ana about stopping around fifty-two or fifty-three instead of sixty-plus. I'd put more into my super, the retirement fund, each year. And I'd still be at every union meeting, because the young ones on my crew won't have the cushion I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more for the young drivers than for me. For myself, a bit calmer than I expected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be all right. What does the end of that decade actually look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably me at the pit gate on my last shift, handing my keys to a guy who'll be watching a screen in an air-conditioned room. I'd want to drive the last real truck out of there, that's the stupid romantic bit. Then I'd go fishing, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the young drivers, what would you want for them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long enough to train them properly for something, fitting, electrical, whatever lasts. I'd want the company paying for that, not leaving it to luck. Kids like Jaz, she's twenty-four and the best new driver I've had, she shouldn't have to find out on a Monday morning.

S4.say: Femi would say a decade leaves no excuse for anyone to be thrown on the scrap heap. He'd want the government, company and union to plan the transition pit by pit, and he'd tell his local member of parliament so.
S4.think: Privately he thinks ten years is a different story, since he'd be 53 with the mortgage paid and the kids out of school. He could drive until near the end and stop, with savings and Ana's pension to lean on.
S4.do: Starts planning with Ana to stop work around 52 or 53 and puts more into his retirement fund each year. Keeps attending union meetings to fight for company-paid training for younger drivers.
S4.feel: Uneasy for the young drivers on his crew, but calmer than he expected about himself.
S4.quote: I'd want to drive the last real truck out of there, that's the stupid romantic bit.
S4.fieldNote: For Femi the extra time turns a threat into an early retirement, because his life stage and savings line up with it. His fight shifts to the young drivers like Jaz, who lack his cushion. He admits the romance in wanting to drive the last truck out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. It's the only one where I don't get to finish on my own terms. What would help is a law that makes the companies share what they save, a proper fund that pays out to workers like me and pays for the young ones to retrain, and a union that's at the table from day one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the town. Our football club, the pub, the bakery on the main street, they all live off miners' wages. If the trucks drive themselves, it's not just my job, it's whether this place still has a reason to exist.

headlineQuote: Every year there's another box with another screen telling me how to drive a road I've driven for nineteen years.
portrait: Femi Wagner is a 43-year-old haul truck crew lead and union shop steward at a large copper pit, with a nurse partner, two kids and a mortgage that's nearly tamed. He's among the best drivers on site, proud of a feel for the road no screen can match, and he has never used an AI tool. In every scenario his instinct is to fight through the union rather than change himself, and he knows it. The two-year AGI picture leaves him angry and alarmed, while the ten-year one turns into a planned early retirement. His deepest concern is for younger drivers and for the town that lives on miners' wages.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it's the only picture where he doesn't get to finish his working life on his own terms.
whatWouldHelp: A law making companies share their savings through a fund that pays out to displaced workers and pays for young workers to retrain, with the union at the table from day one.
